text: And why, thirty five years later, the thing everybody laughed at is still standing, still sealed, and still running experiments nobody else on Earth can run.
To understand how a building like this gets built, you have to go back to a ranch in New Mexico, twenty two years earlier.

text: In nineteen sixty nine, a man named John Polk Allen founded an intentional community fifteen miles south of Santa Fe. He called it Synergia Ranch.

Allen was not a hippie drifter. He had a degree in metallurgical and mining engineering from the Colorado School of Mines, and an M B A from Harvard Business School. He also wrote poetry under the name Johnny Dolphin, and ran a theatre troupe called the Theater of All Possibilities.

text: In the early nineteen seventies the group founded something called the Institute of Ecotechnics. They built a research ship. They ran projects on four continents.

text: And somewhere in that decade, at that ranch, John Allen met Ed Bass, heir to a Fort Worth oil fortune, and one of the wealthiest men in Texas.
In nineteen eighty four they launched the project together. Bass paid. Allen invented. And a designer and architect named Margret Augustine ran the company that would build it.
Here is where the story splits, and where I have to be careful with you, because almost everyone in it is still alive.

In nineteen ninety one, a reporter for the Village Voice named Marc Cooper published a piece about the people behind Biosphere Two. He wrote that they were not, in his words, a group of high tech researchers on the cutting edge of science.
They were, he wrote, a clique of recycled theatre performers that had evolved out of an authoritarian, and decidedly non scientific, personality cult.

That sentence did more damage to Biosphere Two than any scientific result ever did. It is quoted in almost every article written about the project since. And it is an allegation, by a named journalist, in a named magazine. It is not a finding.
Because here is the part that almost never gets quoted alongside it.

The most credentialed early critic of the project was a botanist named Ghillean Prance, the director of the Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew. In nineteen eighty three he said their interest in science was not genuine, that they seemed guided by some sort of religious or philosophical system.
Prance then designed their rainforest.
And in nineteen ninety one, asked about it again, he said this. They are visionaries. And maybe to fulfil their vision they have become somewhat cultlike. But they are not a cult, per se.
source: Ghillean Prance, Phoenix New Times, June 1991
cap: “They are not a cult, per se.”

text: The man who first used the word took it back. Both of those things are on the record, and if you only ever hear one of them, you are not being told the story. You are being sold a verdict.
In nineteen eighty seven, Discover magazine called Biosphere Two the most exciting scientific project undertaken in the United States since Kennedy launched us toward the Moon.
In nineteen ninety two, the journal Ecology called it New Age drivel masquerading as science.
Same building. Five years apart. Both of those are real quotes, and the truth is somewhere in the middle, and the only way to find it is to look at what the building actually did.
